title: Measure it yourself
subtitle: Find Barnard's Star in real SPHEREx images, click it in each epoch and calculate how fast it moves across the sky. Then compare your result with the one Destello and the Gaia catalog give.

player.how1: Look for Barnard's Star in the image. It is the star that is not in the same place in every epoch. Click its centre, or focus the image and move the crosshair with the arrow keys (Shift moves five pixels at a time).
player.how2: Press Confirm, or Enter, to keep the click. You can redo a click at any time.
player.how3: Repeat for every epoch. When you have clicked two or more, the calculation appears below.
player.orientation: North is up and East is to the left. All epochs of the same detector use the same brightness scale.
player.pending: Crosshair at RA {{ra}}, Dec {{dec}}. Press Confirm or Enter to keep it.
player.savedState: Click saved for this epoch. Click the image again, or press Redo, to change it.
player.waiting: Click the star in this epoch.

steps.title: Your measurement, step by step
steps.usesEnds: You clicked {{n}} epochs. To keep the arithmetic simple, the calculation uses only the first and the last of them.
steps.needTwo: Click the star in at least two epochs. So far: {{n}} of {{total}}.
steps.noTime: The epochs you clicked have the same observation time, so no speed can be calculated.

s1.title: Positions
s1.body: Each click was turned into a position on the sky with the map of the image. RA (right ascension) works like longitude and Dec (declination) like latitude. Both are in degrees.

s2.title: How far it moved
s2.body: Subtract the first position from the last one, then change degrees into arcseconds (1 degree is 3600 arcseconds).
s2.cos: RA lines get closer together away from the equator, so a step in RA is shorter on the sky by the cosine of the declination ({{dec}}°, cosine {{cos}}), and we multiply by it.

s3.title: How long it took
s3.body: The time between the two epochs comes from the observation times of the frames: {{first}} and {{last}}.

s4.title: Divide distance by time
s4.body: Dividing each distance by the time gives the speed across the sky in arcseconds per year.

s5.title: Total speed and direction
s5.body: The east-west and north-south parts are at right angles, so the total follows from Pythagoras: the square root of the sum of their squares.
s5.direction: The star moved toward the {{compass}}, {{angle}}° measured from north toward east.

compare.title: How does it compare?
compare.caption: Your proper motion next to Destello's own fit and the catalog value
compare.why: A click and a fit differ because SPHEREx pixels are about 6 arcsec wide, so a click can be off by a good part of a pixel, and this simple calculation ignores parallax, the small yearly shift in position caused by the motion of the Earth.

guide.title: Measure the proper motion of Barnard's Star
guide.lead: A 40 minute lesson in which students measure how fast a star moves across the sky using real SPHEREx images, and compare the result with a catalog value. It needs one computer or tablet for each pair of students.
objectiveList: Read a real astronomical image: orientation, brightness scale and observation dates.
Turn positions in an image into sky coordinates and calculate a speed from a difference in position and a time.
Compare a measurement with a reference value and explain why they are not identical.

intro.title: Introduction
intro.body: Explain that stars drift across the sky very slowly and that Barnard's Star is the fastest known. Ask how this could be measured.

look.title: Look at the images
look.body: In pairs, open the activity and step through the epochs. Ask what changes and what stays the same.

click.title: Click the star
click.body: Each pair clicks the star in every epoch, by mouse or with the keyboard, and confirms each click.

calc.title: Follow the calculation
calc.body: Read the five steps together. Pairs check one number by hand with a calculator.

compare.title: Compare and discuss
compare.body: Pairs write down their result and the comparison table, then discuss the questions below.

materialList: One computer or tablet with a web browser for each pair of students.
A calculator for each pair (optional, to check one step by hand).
Paper and a pencil to write down the result.
stepList: Open the Measure it yourself page and choose the language of the class.
Show the first image and explain that north is up and east is to the left.
Ask each pair to click the star in every epoch and to confirm each click.
Ask them to read the steps under the images and to write down their total proper motion and its direction.
Ask them to read the comparison table and to find the percentage difference with Destello's fit and the catalog value.
questionList: Why does the position of the star change between epochs while the faint background stars stay in place?
What would happen to your result if one click were off by one pixel? Is a longer time between epochs better?
Why is a result from a click different from a fit made by a program?
Why do we multiply the change in RA by the cosine of the declination?
What other measurements could improve the result?
guide.range: A careful class should find a total proper motion of about {{center}} {{unit}}, within a range of {{low}} to {{high}} {{unit}}.
guide.rangeWhy: The centre is the catalog value. The range is the effect of a click error of one image pixel ({{px}} arcsec) at each end, over the {{years}} years between the first and last epoch.
